label: q025a1e284c11d9d0
name: Taputapuatea Marae
value: Taputapuatea Marae is a monumental open-air temple complex on the southeastern coast of Raiatea, the second largest of the Society Islands in French Polynesia. Dedicated to the god 'Oro, it served as the religious and political center of Eastern Polynesia, where chiefs, warriors, and priests from across the Polynesian Triangle gathered for ceremonies. The site represents an exceptional testimony to 1,000 years of Ma'ohi civilization. Inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site on 9 July 2017, it was the first cultural site in a French overseas territory to receive this distinction.

label: q07e60f8366b4e7aa
name: Ringlemere Barrow
value: The Ringlemere barrow is an archaeological site near Sandwich in the English county of Kent most famous as being the find site of the Ringlemere gold cup [1]. No contemporary burials have been found at the site although later Iron Age ones have since been found along with a Saxon cemetery [1]. Excavation work has continued at the site, funded by English Heritage, the BBC, the British Museum and the Kent Archaeological Society [1]. This work has indicated that the now ploughed-away barrow was as high as 5m and had a diameter of more than 40m [1]. The flat-bottomed ditch that surrounded it was 5–6 m wide and 1.35 m deep [1]. Considerable evidence of much earlier Neolithic activity has now been found on the site including by far the largest assemblage of grooved ware in the county [1].

label: q084529e791c4e025
name: Cave of Zeus, Naxos
value: A large cave on the western slope of Mount Zas on Naxos, the highest peak in the Cyclades at 1,003 m, situated at 630 m elevation. The cave entrance widens to approximately 10 meters and extends about 75 meters deep, featuring impressive stalactites and stalagmites. Systematic excavations beginning in 1962 revealed artifacts spanning the Late Neolithic to the Early Cycladic III period, including copper tools now displayed in the Naxos Archaeological Museum. Greek mythology holds that the infant Zeus was hidden here from his father Kronos, and an archaic inscription on the path reads 'Oros Dios Milosiou' (Mountain of Zeus of Milon), attesting to ancient shepherd worship of Zeus.

label: q09a98dc2e23f1279
name: Pyramid of Neferirkare
value: The Pyramid of Neferirkare is the tallest structure at the Abusir necropolis, built for the Fifth Dynasty pharaoh Neferirkare Kakai in the 25th century BC. With a base of 105 m, it was initially designed as a step pyramid with six levels before conversion to a true pyramid was attempted but left incomplete at the king's death. The mortuary temple yielded the Abusir Papyri -- hieratic texts detailing funerary cult management, building activities, and priestly duties -- which also helped archaeologists locate the pyramid of Neferirkare's son Neferefre.

label: q0a27deed6877149a
name: Bokerley Dyke
value: Bokerley Dyke is a linear earthwork 5.75 km long on Cranborne Chase in Dorset, running along the county border with Hampshire between Woodyates and Martin. It may have originated in the Bronze Age as a political boundary, and was cut through by the Roman road Ackling Dyke in the 1st century AD. In the 4th century it was remodelled and the Roman road blocked, dated by a coin of Valens to shortly after 364 AD, possibly in response to the Great Conspiracy of 367-368 AD. It was excavated by Augustus Pitt Rivers between 1888 and 1891 and is a Scheduled Monument.

label: q0e3de7921a88f622
name: Wet Withens
value: Wet Withens is a Bronze Age embanked stone circle on Eyam Moor in the Derbyshire Peak District, and the largest of its type in the county. The continuous bank measures approximately 31m by 29.5m internally, with ten or eleven millstone grit uprights set at the inner edge. Seven stones remain standing, the tallest being the 0.7m 'Chair Stone' in the northeast, which bears possible cupmarks. The circle has a notable midsummer sunrise alignment with Higgar Tor, and the Chair Stone mirrors the shape of the tor on the horizon. The site is a Scheduled Monument, also known as Eyam Moor I.

The fortress seems to have been constructed in stone from the first with a hall-keep surrounded with curtain walls and square towers [1].

name: Sitio Arqueológico Iximche
value: Iximcheʼ is a Pre-Columbian Mesoamerican archaeological site in the western highlands of Guatemala. It served as the capital of the Late Postclassic Kaqchikel Maya kingdom from 1470 until its abandonment in 1524[1]. The site features pyramid-temples, palaces, and two Mesoamerican ballcourts[1]. Excavators uncovered poorly preserved painted murals on some buildings and ample evidence of human sacrifice[1]. The ruins were declared a Guatemalan National Monument in the 1960s and the site now includes a museum displaying sculptures and ceramics found there[1].

label: q19090a138e995a6c
name: Temple of Hephaestus
value: The Temple of Hephaestus or Hephaisteion (also "Hephesteum" or "Hephaesteum"; Ancient Greek: Ἡφαιστεῖον, Greek: Ναός Ηφαίστου, and formerly called in error the Theseion or "Theseum"; Ancient Greek: Θησεῖον, Greek: Θησείο), is a well-preserved Greek temple dedicated to Hephaestus; it remains standing largely intact today [1]. It is a Doric peripteral temple, and is located at the north-west side of the Agora of Athens, on top of the Agoraios Kolonos hill [1]. Archaeological evidence suggests that there was no earlier building on the site except for a small sanctuary that was burned during the Second Persian invasion of Greece in 480 BC [1]. Construction started in 449 BC, and some scholars believe the building not to have been completed for some three decades [1]. The dimensions of the temple are 13.71 m north to south and 31.78 m east to west [1]. Only 18 of the 68 external metopes were sculpted; ten on the east front showed the Labors of Heracles [1].

value: Capital of ancient Mesopotamia on the Euphrates, about 85 km south of Baghdad, Iraq. Under Nebuchadnezzar II (605-561 BC), the city was rebuilt with the famous Ishtar Gate adorned with glazed brick reliefs. It fell to Cyrus the Great in 539 BC and later to Alexander the Great, who died there in 323 BC. Inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2019.

value: Mamai-Hora is the largest multicomplex burial mound in the Northern Black Sea region, located near Velyka Znamianka in Zaporizhzhia Oblast, Ukraine. Spanning millennia of use from the Eneolithic period through the Cossack era, excavations have uncovered over 500 burials across Bronze Age, Scythian, Sarmatian, and medieval periods. Scythian burials yielded weapons, gold items, jewelry, and horse harnesses, including a series of 12 Amazon warrior graves containing arrows and mirrors. Since 2022, the site has been under Russian occupation, threatening its preservation.

label: q25ed0d151fe04d51
name: Templo de Bel
value: The Temple of Bel, sometimes also referred to as the "Temple of Baal", was an ancient temple located in Palmyra, Syria [1]. The temple, consecrated to the Mesopotamian god Bel, worshipped at Palmyra in triad with the lunar god Aglibol and the sun god Yarhibol, formed the center of religious life in Palmyra and was dedicated in AD 32 [1]. The temple was closed during the persecution of pagans in the late Roman Empire in a campaign against the temples of the East made by Maternus Cynegius between 25 May 385 to 19 March 388 [1]. The temple was built on a tell with stratification indicating human occupation that goes back to the third millennium BC [1]. The walls of the temenos and propylaea were constructed in the late first and the first half of the second century AD [1]. The Temple of Bel was converted into a Christian church during the Byzantine Era [1].

label: q26a1ed90835a859a
name: Ramesses III Temple
value: The Mortuary Temple of Ramesses III at Medinet Habu is a well-preserved New Kingdom temple on the West Bank of Luxor, Egypt, built in the 12th century BC [1]. Covering over 7,000 m², this "million-year house" served the divine cult of the pharaoh Ramesses III [1]. The temple complex also includes an Amun temple, burial chapels of the divine wives of Amun from the 23rd–26th dynasties, and a sacred lake [1]. It is renowned for its relief depictions of Ramesses III's victory over the Sea Peoples around 1175 BC [1][2].

name: Sunningdale Barrow
value: Sunningdale Barrow is an archaeological site in Berkshire, England, comprising three Bronze Age round barrows. One bowl barrow is located near Sunningdale railway station, in an area historically part of Surrey before boundary changes. Excavations during the 19th century uncovered cremation burials, the majority of which were placed in pottery urns, reflecting typical Bronze Age funerary practices in southern England where cremation increasingly replaced earlier inhumation customs. These barrows represent important ritual landscapes utilized by prehistoric communities over several centuries.

label: q30afbd2f0fe6c2a5
name: Castlesteads, Greater Manchester
value: Castlesteads is a late Iron Age promontory fort on the east bank of the River Irwell in Bury, Greater Manchester. Occupied from the 5th century BC into the Roman period, the fort exploits steep natural slopes on three sides, with a 6-metre-wide, 120-metre-long defensive ditch protecting the eastern approach. Excavations in the 1960s-1990s uncovered postholes from Iron Age roundhouses and pottery consistent with Brigantian wares from the 1st century AD. The fort likely survived the Roman invasion because Queen Cartimandua of the Brigantes was a Roman client ruler. Radiocarbon dating of charcoal confirmed occupation around 2,000 years ago.

value: The Anta da Pedra dos Mouros, also known as the Anta do Senhor da Serra, is a megalithic dolmen situated near Belas and Queluz in the Lisbon District of Portugal [1]. The Anta da Pedra dos Mouros, the Anta da Estria, and the Anta do Monte Abraão are a short distance from each other and are collectively known as the Antas de Belas [1]. The Anta da Pedra dos Mouros was reportedly first identified in 1856 by Carlos Ribeiro but he did not have a chance to carry out excavations until 1876 after receiving approval from the landowner [1]. The burial chamber was at that time already in bad condition, having only three upright support stones, with one apparently having two anthropomorphic figures engraved on it [1]. Items found by Ribeiro during his excavations are kept in the Geological Museum in Lisbon [1]. They include a stone axe, flint tools, utensils for domestic use, vases, and human and animal bones [1].

value: Ruins of a prosperous colony on the north Aegean island of Thasos, founded around 680-650 BC by settlers from Paros led by Telesicles, father of the poet Archilochus. The city grew wealthy from gold mines on the mainland yielding 200-300 talents annually, plus marble quarries and wine exports. The ancient agora, developed from the 6th century BC onward, preserves the cenotaph of the early settler Glaucus. Massive marble-faced city walls, a Classical-era theatre, and temples to Heracles and Athena survive among the ruins.

name: Casma-Sechin Culture
value: The Casma–Sechin culture (c. 3600 BCE–200 BCE) of Peru refers to the large concentration of pre-historic ruins in the valleys of the Casma River and its tributary the Sechin River and along the nearby coast of the Pacific Ocean [1]. The ruins include major archaeological sites such as Sechin Bajo, Sechin Alto, Cerro Sechin, Mojeque, Chankillo, and Taukachi-Konkan, as well as other smaller sites [1]. Most of these inland sites are found in the river valleys about 20 kilometres distant from the ocean [1]. The seaside sites of Huaynuná and Las Haldas are found about 20 kilometres north and south of the mouth of the Casma River on the coast [1]. The area of the Casma/Sechin culture extended about 40 kilometres inland from the sea [1]. By 3000 BC, at a few locations in coastal Peru, including the Casma/Sechin valleys, a sizable population was present and undertaking large projects such as building pyramids and other ceremonial and monumental structures [1]. Radiocarbon dating indicates a plaza at Sechin Bajo was constructed in 3500 BCE [1].

value: Romano-Celtic temple discovered in 1959 from cropmarks near Wymondham, Norfolk. label: q78d29783d86cc324

value: Ptolemais was one of the five cities forming the Pentapolis of Cyrenaica, founded by a Ptolemaic king, probably Ptolemy III Euergetes (246-221 BC), on the site of an earlier Greek port for the city of Barca. The planned city enclosed 280 hectares within walls measuring approximately 1,650 by 1,400 metres, and contained a hippodrome, amphitheatre, and three theatres. Under Diocletian it became capital of the province of Libya Superior, surpassing Cyrene. Its ruins at modern Tolmeita are on the UNESCO Tentative List.

label: qab264b062271691a
name: Hierapolis
value: An ancient Greco-Roman city at Pamukkale in southwestern Turkey, founded as a formal city under the Seleucid Empire in the 2nd century BC on the site of a 7th-century BC Phrygian temple to Cybele. Famous for its thermal hot springs, the city features a remarkably preserved 15,000-seat Roman theatre, the Temple of Apollo, the toxic-gas Plutonium, and one of the largest ancient necropolises in Anatolia. A UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1988, Hierapolis was also a major early Christian centre where the Apostle Philip was martyred.

label: qac11398e15f1e226
name: Tayma Stones
value: The Tayma stones are Aramaic stelae discovered at the oasis of Tayma in northern Saudi Arabia, dating to approximately the 5th century BC. The first stela was uncovered in 1880 by Charles Huber and is now in the Louvre; a second was found in 1980 and remains in Saudi Arabia. The inscriptions reference Syrian and Mesopotamian deities including Salm, Ashima, and Asherah, reflecting lasting cultural influence from Babylonian king Nabonidus, who made Tayma his capital-in-exile in the mid-6th century BC. Over twenty inscriptions have been published since 1884, providing key evidence of Aramaic language and religious syncretism in ancient Arabia.

label: qafe24a4da029ccc3
name: Lukyanus Kitabesi
value: The Lukyanus Inscription and Equestrian Rock Relief is a Roman-period monument (1st–4th c. AD) in Konya Province, Turkey. It features a 1.85‑metre‑long horse relief carved on a steep rock face together with a niche, both situated approximately 10 metres above ground level [1]. To the right, a ten‑line Greek inscription measuring 0.85 × 0.95 metres is positioned about 5 metres from the ground [1]. The inscription records horse races to be held in honor of a young cavalryman who died, including the rules governing these races [1].

label: qb023332af4253f01
name: Amelungsburg, Süntel
value: The Amelungsburg is a former Celtic ringfort (hillfort) on the Amelungsberg hill in the Süntel ridge, Lower Saxony, Germany, dating to 500 BC–1 AD [1]. The site covers approximately 15 hectares on a plateau 900 metres long and 300 metres wide, with steep cliffs on all sides providing natural defense [1]. The fortifications consist of a rampart extending about 1,000 metres along two sides of the terrain [1]. Archaeological evidence indicates Iron Age habitation, making it one of the largest hillforts in northern Germany [1].

label: qb193b7cb36678571
name: Devetashka Cave
value: Devetashka Cave is a massive karst formation near the village of Devetaki in northern Bulgaria, measuring approximately 2 km in length with a cavernous entrance hall reaching 60 m in height and seven natural ceiling openings known as 'the eyes'. Archaeological evidence reveals nearly continuous human occupation spanning 70,000 years, from the Middle Paleolithic to the Late Neolithic. The sediment layers have yielded one of the richest sources of Neolithic cultural artifacts (6th-4th millennium BC) in Bulgaria, alongside Paleolithic flint tools, Bronze Age battle axes, and Iron Age weapons. Declared a natural landmark in 1996, the cave also shelters nearly 30,000 bats, though military use in the 1950s for petroleum storage damaged some formations.

value: Pachataka (also spelled Pachataca or Pachat'aqa), commonly known as the Inca Gallows, is an archaeological site in Bolivia, located near Lake Titicaca in the municipality of Copacabana, Manco Kapac Province [1]. Pachataka is a pre-Inca astronomical observatory formed by a lintel made of two parallel stone blocks [1]. It was used to determine the seasons, track lunar movements, and predict eclipses [1]. It is located at the summit of Mount Kesanani, approximately 600 meters south of the town of Copacabana [1]. According to mathematical and astronomical calculations conducted by the Institute of Cosmic Physics of Bolivia, the observatory dates approximately to 1764 B.C., during the era of the Chiripa culture [1].

label: qb38c1e37f9f9029b
name: Devil's Lapful
value: Devil's Lapful is a Neolithic long cairn in Kielder Forest, Northumberland, dating to approximately 3400-2400 BC. One of few surviving long cairns in Northumberland, it measures 60 by 14 metres and stands 2 metres high, constructed of rounded boulders with stone slabs and smaller stones at the edges. Oriented north-northeast to south-southwest on a hillside slope, the cairn likely served as a communal burial site for a local community over several generations. First examined in the 1930s by Newbigin with inconclusive results, the site shows evidence of later quarrying for a nearby sheep fold. It has been designated a scheduled monument.

label: qb8a40206a2446072
name: The Acropolis of Ancient Thasos
value: The Acropolis of ancient Thasos crowns a hilltop at 137 metres above the town of Limenas on the island of Thasos, Greece, with origins dating to the 7th century BC when colonists from Paros settled the island. The second summit holds a temple dedicated to Athena dating from the early 5th century BC, while the highest peak contains a sanctuary to the god Pan with an anaglyph depicting him with hoofs and pipes carved directly into the rock. Armoured marble fortification walls were built by the island's first inhabitants and later reconstructed across multiple periods by Persians, Macedonians, and Romans. Excavations have uncovered pottery, jewelry, coins, and the foundations of an ancient theatre.

label: qba41430e1468e228
name: Cave of Gabrovnica
value: The Cave of Gabrovnica near Knjazevac in eastern Serbia contains the only known prehistoric cave paintings in the country. Discovered in 1997 by researchers from the Belgrade Faculty of Philosophy and the Knjazevac Homeland Museum, the cave holds five black charcoal drawings: two horses with riders, a horse with a dagger above its neck, an irregular circle, and one unclear figure. Dating to 3,000-4,000 years ago at the transition from the Bronze Age to the Iron Age, the dagger type depicted helps confirm the chronology. One horseman drawing was damaged by vandals with a sharp object in 2018.

label: qbab62bca9b69a449
name: Agios Vasileios, Laconia
value: Agios Vasileios is the site of a Mycenaean palace, located 4 kilometers east of the village of Xirokambi in Laconia [1]. It was west of the Eurotas River commanding the plain, some 10 km south of Sparta [1]. Ayios Vasileios was lightly inhabited during the Early Helladic I–II period (c. 3200-2200 BC) then abandoned for a time [1]. It was re-occupied in the Middle Helladic III period (c. 1700–1550 BC), again lightly [1]. The site grew in the Late Helladic period (c. 1550–1050 BC) reaching a maximum size of about 20 hectares before facing destruction and abandonment [1]. Excavations, carried out by the Archaeological Society of Athens and directed by archaeologist Adamantia Vasilogamvrou, began in 2009 [1].

value: The Miami Circle, also known as The Miami River Circle, Brickell Point, or The Miami Circle at Brickell Point Site, is an archaeological site in Brickell, Miami, Florida [1]. On February 5, 2002, the site was listed on the National Register of Historic Places [1]. It was declared a National Historic Landmark on January 16, 2009 [1]. The Miami-Dade Historic Preservation Division conducted the salvage excavation of the site [1]. In the course of the exploration, the team discovered a number of holes cut into the Oolitic limestone bedrock [1]. Further examination of the artifacts found at the site, particularly the shell tools, shark teeth, and other items of aquatic origin, showed that they matched perfectly with artifacts known to be from a local tribe, the historic Tequesta [1].

value: La Muerta is a Maya archaeological site in the northern Petén region of Guatemala, located between the sites of El Mirador and El Tintal [1]. It is located on a promontory 3.5 kilometres south of the El Tigre complex of El Mirador, and it is considered a satellite of that city [1]. La Muerta was inhabited during the Early to Late Classic Period [1]. La Muerta was investigated by archaeologist Richard D. Hansen in the 1980s [1]. The site is divided into North and South Groups, located approximately 400 metres apart [1]. Eleven residential areas have been identified within these two groups [1]. Structure A1 is a temple with a north-facing stairway [1]. Monument 1 is a sculptured stela that was found in the North Group [1].

value: The Suburban Baths (Terme Suburbane) are a publicly owned Roman bathhouse in Pompeii, Italy, built outside the city walls near the Porta Marina, possibly under Emperor Tiberius (14-37 AD). The three-level complex includes a frigidarium, tepidarium, and calidarium, with a heated swimming pool added after the earthquake of 62 AD. The changing room contains eight erotic frescoes, now interpreted not as evidence of a brothel but as a humorous system for helping bathers remember where they stored their clothes. The baths likely served travelers arriving from the nearby port.

value: Gilwern Hill, about 5 km southeast of Llandrindod Wells in Powys, Wales, hosts a Neolithic-Bronze Age stone circle of approximately 14 stones, half of which have fallen. A small island was formed part-way across the structure, and associated items have led scholars to conclude the island was of religious significance [1]. Archaeological work began in 1982, and the site is located 800 metres east of Fengate [1]. Flag Fen is now part of the Greater Fens Museum Partnership, with a visitor centre on site and some areas reconstructed including an Iron Age roundhouse dwelling [1].

value: The Site de Tiklat is located near El Kseur in Bejaia Province, Algeria, and corresponds to the ancient Roman colony of Tubusuctu. name: Baelo Claudia
value: Baelo Claudia was an ancient Roman town in Hispania, situated on the shore of the Strait of Gibraltar, 22 km outside modern Tarifa in southern Spain [1]. Originally a fishing village and trading hub settled approximately 2,000 years ago, it flourished as a prosperous city during Emperor Claudius's reign before declining due to earthquakes and eventual abandonment by the 6th century [1].

name: Corycus, Crete
value: Corycus (or Korykos) was an ancient town in northwestern Crete, situated on the peninsula of the same name. [1] The settlement is mentioned by the geographer Ptolemy in his works. [1] The Roman poet Juvenal references a Corycian vessel, confirming the town's maritime significance in the classical period. [1] When Florentine traveler Cristoforo Buondelmonti visited Crete in 1415, he documented that remains of the ancient town still existed. [1]
